captions.text: The school garden tank is filling.
A rising line looks promising, but can we promise what the tank will hold tomorrow?
Picture two garden tanks beside the school vegetable beds.
Rain adds water and watering the plants removes it.
A class records the amount on the same four school days.
A line graph can help us follow change, but only when we know what its axes and units mean.
Today we are learning to interpret line graphs and explain what their evidence supports.
Our goal is to interpret observations over time and make careful comparisons.
We want to read a particular day, calculate a change between days, and explain which conclusions are supported.
Keep those three different jobs separate as we build the graph.
I can read the time axis and the labelled scale.
I can compare changes over equal time intervals.
I can separate observations from uncertain predictions.
Remember reading a table by matching a row label with a quantity.
We will turn those table observations into points.
Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday belong in time order.
Equal spaces along the time axis will represent equal one-day intervals.
A line graph shows observations in time order.
The horizontal axis shows time and the vertical axis shows the measured quantity and unit.
Equal spaces must mean equal time intervals.
Read the scale before comparing heights.
A rising segment means an increase, a falling one a decrease and a flat one no change.
The line connects observations; it does not prove every value between them or any future value.
Start with the horizontal time axis.
Add the days in order and leave equal spacing.
The vertical axis measures litres, starting at zero and increasing by ten litres at each marked interval.
Plot Monday at ten, Tuesday at twenty, Wednesday at twenty and Thursday at forty.
Join consecutive observations so the segments show changes between recorded days.
A tank holds 10, 20, 20 and 40 litres on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.
Which equal daily interval rose most?
Before deciding which increase is largest, look at each pair of neighbouring days.
Predict the change from Monday to Tuesday, then from Tuesday to Wednesday, and finally from Wednesday to Thursday.
Keep your three changes in mind.
Which interval do you think has the greatest increase?
Changes are +10 L, 0 L and +20 L.
Wednesday to Thursday rose most.
The highest point and the largest rise answer different questions.
Tuesday’s twenty litres minus Monday’s ten gives an increase of ten litres.
The two middle readings are equal, so that interval has no change.
Thursday’s forty minus Wednesday’s twenty gives an increase of twenty litres.
That last rise is greatest.
The highest reading and the largest change are different questions.
Tank B: 20,20,30,30 L on the same days.
Which is fuller on Thursday?
Can we promise Friday?
Tank B has twenty, twenty, thirty and thirty litres on the same days.
It uses the same time and quantity scales.
Before we reveal a comparison, find Thursday on both lines and read the two values.
Which tank is fuller, and what subtraction will tell you the difference?
A has 40 L and B has 30 L on Thursday, a difference of 10 L.
We need new observations for Friday: rain and water use may change.
If a vertical axis starts above zero, a small change can look dramatic; read the labels.
The solid circle line represents A, while the dashed square line represents B.
On Thursday, A has forty litres and B has thirty.
The difference is ten litres.
On Monday, B was fuller instead.
Comparing at the same time is important: a Monday point on one line and a Thursday point on the other answer a different question.
“A rising line must keep rising.” It records what happened during the shown times.
A forecast is uncertain and needs extra evidence.
The line between observations helps us see change, but it does not record every moment.
